blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
World models have become a central component of autonomous driving research.
By predicting future scene states conditioned on ego actions, they support
counterfactual reasoning, closed-loop simulation and model-based planning.
Recent driving world models synthesise future video conditioned on ego
trajectories or high-level commands [ 11 , 22 , 7 ] ,
and planning-oriented approaches learn latent or occupancy dynamics jointly with
a driving policy [ 10 , 26 ] .

blocks.en:
Existing evaluations of these models focus on the fidelity of the generated
futures or on downstream planning performance, and rarely verify that the
predictions depend on the conditioning action.
Over short horizons, however, ego motion is strongly autocorrelated, so the
observed history already encodes much of the information carried by the future
action.
A model trained on logged driving data can therefore attain high forecasting
accuracy while making little use of its action input, a failure mode analogous to
the inertia and copycat problems reported for imitation-learned driving
policies [ 2 , 23 , 4 ] .
An accuracy gain over a model without action input shows that the action is used,
but not how strongly the forecasts depend on it, since on logged data the executed
action and the action implied by the history largely coincide.
How strongly action-conditioned forecasters trained on real driving data depend on
the ego action, and whether this dependence holds across vehicle platforms,
therefore remains largely unexplored.

blocks.en:
To address these questions, we study action dependence in semantic
forecasting [ 12 ] , which predicts future semantic
segmentation from past observations and has an established evaluation protocol
on Cityscapes [ 3 ] .
Conditioning this task on future vehicle odometry has been proposed
before [ 1 ] , but whether the forecaster uses the
odometry was not examined.
We condition on the ego action, represented by speed and yaw rate, and
compare a U-Net forecaster with feature-wise linear modulation
(FiLM) [ 16 ] , input-level conditioning, and no action input.
The rationale is that semantic forecasting has a compact output space and
standard metrics, so each variant can be trained with several seeds at modest
cost and its use of the action can be measured without new evaluation criteria.
To assess whether the findings transfer across vehicle platforms, we define an
equivalent protocol on BDD100K [ 25 ] , which differs from
Cityscapes in camera, ego-motion sensing and driving environment.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Predicting future observations conditioned on actions originates in
action-conditional video prediction for games [ 15 ] and robot
manipulation [ 6 ] , and in world models that learn
behaviour inside a learned simulator [ 8 , 9 ] .
In driving, MILE [ 10 ] learns a latent world model jointly with a
driving policy, OccWorld [ 26 ] forecasts 3D occupancy together
with ego motion, and GAIA-1 [ 11 ] , DriveDreamer [ 22 ] and Vista [ 7 ] synthesise future video conditioned on actions,
trajectories or commands.
A common theme across these works is that evaluation targets the fidelity of the
predicted futures or the performance of a downstream planner.
In contrast, we measure directly whether the prediction depends on the action,
using a model small enough to be trained with multiple seeds.

blocks.en:
Luc et al . [ 12 ] introduced the forecasting of future semantic
segmentation on Cityscapes, with short-term (0.18 s) and mid-term (0.54 s)
horizons that subsequent work adopted.
Follow-up methods forecast with convolutional LSTMs [ 14 ] ,
recurrent flow-guided warping [ 21 ] , or in feature space

These methods condition on past frames only.
Bhattacharyya et al . [ 1 ] additionally condition a
Bayesian forecaster on past and future vehicle odometry, but report no
evaluation of how the predictions depend on it.
Our work extends this line of research by measuring that dependence under the
standard protocol, and by defining an equivalent protocol on a second platform.

Driving policies trained by imitation are known to exploit the ego vehicle’s past
motion instead of the scene, which is referred to as the
inertia [ 2 ] and copycat [ 23 ] problems,
and more generally to rely on spurious correlates of the expert

The forecasting counterpart of this failure mode is a world model that reproduces
the observed motion and treats its action input as optional.
Test-time input interventions provide a direct test for this behaviour, and we
adopt them as our primary evaluation.

blocks.en:
Cityscapes [ 3 ] contains 30-frame video snippets recorded
at approximately 17 Hz, with fine annotations (gtFine) for the 20th frame and
vehicle odometry for every frame.
We follow the standard forecasting protocol [ 12 ] : frames 8,
11, 14 and 17 are used to predict frame 20 (short term, Δ = 0.18 \Delta{=}0.18 s), and
frames 2, 5, 8 and 11 to predict frames 14, 17 and 20 (mid term, 0.54 s).
Models are trained on the 2,975 training snippets and evaluated on the 500
validation snippets against gtFine at 1024 × 2048 1024{\times}2048 .
Speed and yaw rate are taken from the vehicle odometry.

One sample is drawn every 2 s of each clip.

blocks.en: 4.2 Implementation details
blocks.zh: 4.2 执行细节

blocks.en:
Inputs are resized to 256 × 512 256{\times}512 on Cityscapes and 288 × 512 288{\times}512 on
BDD100K, and predictions are bilinearly upsampled to the evaluation resolution.
All models are trained from scratch with AdamW (learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight
decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ), a one-cycle schedule and a batch size of 16, for 60 epochs on
Cityscapes and 12 epochs on BDD100K, with horizontal-flip augmentation
( Eq. 7 ).
Each variant is trained with three random seeds, and we report the mean and
standard deviation.
We compare with two baselines that use no action: copy-last, which repeats the last
observed segmentation, and flow warping, which extrapolates the optical
flow [ 5 ] between the last two context frames to warp the last
segmentation.
On Cityscapes, we also report published results on the same
protocol [ 12 , 1 , 18 ] .

Across both datasets, the action-conditioned forecasters acquire a dependence on the
action that far exceeds the accuracy it adds.
On Cityscapes, FiLM gains 2.46 mid-term mIoU from the executed action but loses

The accuracy gain over the no-action model shows that the action is used; the
interventions show how strongly the forecasts depend on it.
They measure the strength of this dependence, not whether it is correct.
The executed action gives the highest accuracy in every in-domain setting, and in Fig. 1 only the executed turn moves the scene as observed, which
indicates that the dependence acts in the right direction; a stronger dependence,
however, is not desirable in itself.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
In this work, we studied how strongly action-conditioned semantic forecasters depend
on the ego action.
By replacing the future action at test time and scoring the forecasts with standard
segmentation metrics, we measured action dependence for feature-wise, input-level and
no action conditioning, after validating the interventions in a synthetic
environment.
Experiments on Cityscapes and BDD100K show that the executed action improves
mid-term mIoU by at most 2.46 points, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.17
points, below the model without action input.
On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than
input-level conditioning, but not in the synthetic environment, where the history
does not determine the action.
These findings show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses
its action but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it, so action dependence
should be measured explicitly.
In future work, we plan to apply history-consistent interventions to larger video and
occupancy world models over longer horizons and to relate action dependence to
planning performance.
